name: Iris Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Eastfield Homes, a housing association, so we rent out about 1,400 flats to people on lower incomes. I get in at half eight, check the repairs diary, book the plumbers and electricians into slots, and file the tenancy paperwork that comes in. I like knowing where everything is; I've got a colour system for the paper files that nobody else understands but everyone relies on.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The phone, mostly, and the new case system they brought in last spring. It keeps logging me out and I end up writing things on a pad first and typing them in later. My partner Sam drives the number 14 bus, so we're both on shifts and I'm usually the one cooking at seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what's happening now. A lot of noise and a few new buttons on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at work: the tenants need people, not chatbots. When Mrs Okafor rings about her boiler, she wants someone who knows her block. I'd probably post something like that in the union group chat too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not relaxed. Our budget's been cut two years running and they froze one admin post already, so AI or no AI, management is looking for savings. If the routine stuff like booking repairs gets automated even a little, that's the part of my day they'd point at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down, and I'd stay in the union because that's what protects us when they restructure. I'd also try to put another £100 a month into savings, because our rent went up £60 in September. I won't be learning any AI tools; I'd rather be really good at the things I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired. It's not fear of robots, it's the same worry I have every year when the budget comes out in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the repairs booking is the part they'd point at. How much of your day is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe half of it, if I'm honest. Booking, rebooking, chasing the contractor, ringing the tenant back. The other half is filing and the people stuff, like calming someone down at the front desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway on Fridays and the gym I never go to. Sam would say the gym is mine and the takeaway is his, so we'd argue about that first.

say: The tenants need **real people**, not chatbots, when something breaks at home.
I'd post in the **union group chat** that cuts are a choice, not a technology.
think: Even small automation hits the **repairs booking**, which is half my day.
The **budget cuts** worry me more than AI, because one post is already frozen.
do: Stay in the **union** and keep my head down at work.
Put an extra **£100 a month** into savings after the rent rise.
Skip **AI tools** and stay sharp at the filing and front desk.
feel: Tired and **wary**, the same feeling as every **March budget**.
S0.quote: AI or no AI, management is looking for savings.
fieldNote: Her worry here comes from **budget cuts** that already happened, not from the technology.
She says half her day is **routine booking**, which makes even a small change feel close.
She refuses to touch AI and frames **skill at the familiar** as her protection.

steps.text: Stay a paid-up member of the housing union
Save an extra £100 a month after the rent rise
Keep booking repairs and filing the same way as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can actually see happening. They'd love that at head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: if they use AI to book repairs, the savings should go to the tenants, not the directors. I'd want the union to push for an agreement that nobody gets pushed out without retraining. I'd probably say that at the staff meeting, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is exactly the kind they mean. Booking, checking, answering tenants: that's the list on the card. The other admin, Paula, has been there eleven years and knows the system better than me, so if they keep one of us, I'm not sure it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask my manager straight out what the plan is for admin roles, in writing. I'd cut the takeaways and the gym that month and try to get our savings from about three months to five. If they offered training, I'd probably go, even though I'd hate it, but I'd also start looking at the council's tenancy officer jobs, which are more face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like when you hear your name in a meeting you weren't invited to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council's tenancy officer jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's going out to estates, knocking on doors, sitting in someone's kitchen sorting out a dispute. A computer can book a plumber, but it can't calm down two neighbours arguing about a dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate the training. What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not clever with computers and they know it. Sam would tell me I run that whole office and I should stop talking myself down, which is what he always says.

say: Any **savings from AI** should go to tenants, not to the directors.
The **union** should win a deal that nobody goes without retraining.
think: My job is the **exact list** on the card: booking, checking and answering.
If they keep one admin, **Paula** probably stays because she knows the system better.
do: Ask my manager **in writing** what happens to admin roles.
Grow savings from about **three to five months** by cutting takeaways and the gym.
Apply for council **tenancy officer** jobs that are face to face.
feel: Sick in the stomach, like being **discussed** in a meeting I'm not in.
S1.quote: A computer can book a plumber, but it can't calm down two neighbours arguing about a dog.
fieldNote: She sees her own task list in the card and expects **fewer admin posts**.
Publicly she argues about **who gets the savings**; privately she ranks herself below a colleague.
Her escape route is **face-to-face work**, not technology, which fits her dislike of new tools.

steps.text: Ask the housing manager in writing about plans for admin roles
Cut takeaways and the gym to reach five months of savings
Apply for council tenancy officer jobs on the estates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our tenancy runs out. That's before anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government to step in now: a pause, a tax on the companies, money for the people who lose work. I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd tell people at work we should all join the union this week, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm gone. My whole job is thinking work, the boring kind, and the card says that comes first in 2028. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because I don't do anything with my hands except carry boxes of files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food and the bus pass, starting tomorrow. I'd talk to Sam about whether we move in with his mum for a while to stretch the savings. And I'd look hard at care work or anything hands-on, because that gives me those three extra years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'm not someone who changes fast, and two years is faster than I've ever done anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sam's job on the buses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His is hands-on, so he'd get to 2031 maybe, but self-driving buses would be on the list too. That's the bit that keeps me up: both of us gone inside five years, and only about three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work is a big change. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I looked after my nan when she was ill, so I know I can do the washing and the lifting. I'd do it, but I'd be doing it because I had to, not because I wanted it.

say: The government must step in now with a **tax on AI firms** and support.
Everyone at work should **join the union** this week, not next year.
think: My job is all **thinking work**, so I'm gone in 2028.
The **three-year gap** before robots helps hands-on workers, not me with my files.
do: Cut spending to **rent, food** and the bus pass from tomorrow.
Talk to Sam about **moving in** with his mum to stretch savings.
Apply for **care work**, which buys about three years before robots.
feel: **Frightened**, because two years is faster than she's ever changed anything.
S2.quote: My whole job is thinking work, the boring kind, and the card says that comes first in 2028.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and fears her partner's bus job follows.
The **robot gap** matters to her only as a reason to switch to hands-on care.
She falls back on **family housing** and protest, not on new skills.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the bus pass
Move in with Sam's mum for a while to save rent
Apply for home care jobs looking after older people
Join any march calling for an AI tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two, but I keep thinking how slow I am with change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but louder: we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd push our union branch to get something written into contracts by next year. People would roll their eyes at me, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to get comfortable and not do anything, and that's what scares me about myself. I know I'd tell myself next year, next year. By 2031 the office work's gone and I'd be 32 with nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do one real thing in the first year: sign up for a care certificate at the college in the evenings, the one that takes about a year. I'd keep the admin job for the pay while I train. We'd also keep building savings, maybe to six months, instead of booking the trip to see Sam's cousins in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a dentist appointment that's in the diary for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself next year. Who would stop you doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, probably, and my sister Lin, who's a nurse. Lin would book me onto the course herself if she had to, she's that type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paula. She's 54 and she's never done anything else. She'd have five years to go before retirement and nothing to do in them.

say: Five years means **no excuse** for the government not having a plan.
Our union branch should get **job protections** into contracts by next year.
think: Five years is long enough for me to **put things off** until too late.
By 2031 the office work's gone and I'm **32 with nothing new**.
do: Start an **evening care certificate** at the college in the first year.
Keep the **admin pay** while training, and build savings to six months.
Skip the **summer trip** to Sam's cousins to save the money.
feel: A constant **unease**, like a dentist appointment sitting in the diary.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get comfortable and not do anything, and that's what scares me about myself.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the job**, but the extra time gives her a plan.
Her real fear is her own **habit of delay**, which she names herself.
Her sister Lin, a nurse, acts as **the push** she knows she needs.

steps.text: Start an evening care certificate at the local college
Skip the summer trip and build savings to six months
Push the union branch for job protections in contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That feels like a whole different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and that the unions and the government need to plan training now, paid for by the companies making money from this. I'd probably say it at Christmas dinner and start an argument with my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay-ish. Ten years is time to change slowly, and slow is the only way I change. But I still think the admin side of the housing association shrinks a lot well before 2036, so it's not like I'm safe till then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, not much: I'd keep my job and keep saving. Maybe by year two or three I'd do the care certificate or ask about moving into a tenancy officer role inside Eastfield. Sam and I would probably still try to buy a small flat, but somewhere cheaper, further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still a knot. I'd rather it was ten years than two, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the admin side shrinks well before 2036. When do you think it starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four years in, when the software is good enough and cheap enough. Housing associations are always the last to get new stuff, which is the one time being behind helps us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want a family in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years. I think we'd still do it, but I'd want one of us in a job a computer can't do first.

say: Ten years is a **gift if used**, with training paid by the companies profiting.
I'd argue at **Christmas dinner** that the unions and government must plan now.
think: Ten years suits me, because **slow** is the only way I change.
The admin side still **shrinks early**, maybe three or four years in.
do: Keep the job and **keep saving** through the first year.
Ask about a **tenancy officer** role inside Eastfield by year two or three.
Look for a **cheaper flat** to buy further out with Sam.
feel: Calmer, but with a **knot** that hasn't gone away.
S4.quote: Housing associations are always the last to get new stuff, which is the one time being behind helps us.
fieldNote: The decade fits her **slow pace**, but she still expects her admin role to shrink.
She puts a **date** on the risk: three or four years in, not 2036.
She'd want one **safe job** in the household before having children.

steps.text: Keep the admin job and keep saving each month
Ask about moving into a tenancy officer role at Eastfield
Look at cheaper flats further out to buy with Sam

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. What would help is the union having a deal in place before it happens, and some kind of income support while people like me retrain, because I can't retrain and pay rent on three months of savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who decides. Everyone talks about AI like weather, but somebody at head office signs the paper that says which posts go. It's people deciding, not a machine.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like weather, but somebody at head office signs the paper that says which posts go.
portrait: Iris, 27, is an office administrator at **Eastfield Homes**, a housing association, and lives with her partner Sam, a bus driver.
She runs **repairs booking** and paper files, avoids new technology and never uses AI tools.
She sees **budget cuts** and management choices, not machines, as the real threat.
In the fast AGI pictures she expects to **lose her job** and switch to care work.
With ten years she's calmer, because **slow change** is the only kind she trusts herself with.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because her desk job goes first and her partner's bus job may follow.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** in place beforehand and **income support** while she retrains.
